question:
A 56-year-old male with a history of diabetic nephropathy comes to the physician reporting recurrent
episodes of severe abdominal pain over the past four years. The pain is primarily located in the
midabdominal region with occasional radiation to the midback, lasting several hours and showing no
consistent relationship with meals. He also describes progressively worsening intermittent diarrhea for
the past year. The patient denies any substance use. Laboratory tests show anemia with elevated
serum amylase and lipase levels. After prescribing appropriate pain medication and enteric-coated

delayed-release pancrelipase, the physician warns about a specific side effect that requires regular
monitoring. Which laboratory test would be most appropriate for monitoring this particular adverse
effect? Answer Choices: (A) Serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (B) Serum magnesium (C) Serum
ionized calcium (D) Serum albumin (E) Complete blood count (F) Serum alkaline phosphatase (G)
Serum uric acid (H) Serum lipase (I) Serum creatinine (J) Serum amylase
 A. Serum amylase
B. Serum albumin
C. Serum ionized calcium
D. Complete blood count
E. Serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase
F. Serum uric acid
G. Serum creatinine
H. Serum magnesium
I. Serum lipase
J. Serum alkaline phosphatase
